source.title: Optimal Rate of Kernel Regression in Large Dimensions
source.authors: Weihao Lu; Hao Zhang; Yicheng Li; Manyun Xu; Qian Lin

page_placements.theme: Multiple descent and periodic plateaus in kernel convergence-rate exponents

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure labels are flattened or lose mathematical formatting; no apparent cutoff or wrong-document issue.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives multiple-descent and plateau behavior for kernel-regression risk as the sample-size/dimension scaling exponent γ varies. It does not test the claim’s model-size, epoch, or fixed-dimension sample-size axes, nor risk versus capacity past an interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The paper's own theoretical and experimental results concern kernel regression with n ≍ d^γ, and report nonmonotone rates over γ. This is related to, but does not measure, any listed version's specified axis or interpolation-threshold behavior. The stopping-time constants tried to select the reported setting are not separate results. Comparisons and results cited from other work are not recorded as findings here.
record.test_reason: The paper derives minimax excess-risk rates for kernel regression with n ≍ d^γ and calls the non-monotone rate-exponent curve over γ 'multiple descent'. Along γ, sample size and dimension move together. The quantity plotted is a convergence-rate exponent, not a risk value. Nothing is swept along model size, epochs, or samples at a fixed interpolation threshold. No peak is shown being driven by noise or removed by regularization. The experiments compare early-stopped kernel regression with kernel interpolation, not risk across capacity. So no listed version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors derive matching upper and minimax lower bounds for early-stopped kernel regression for all γ > 0, giving rate n^-1/2 at even integer γ. They identify 'multiple descent' and 'periodic plateau' behaviour of the optimal rate curve in γ. They extend the result to the NTK and, as a corollary, to wide neural networks. They argue that kernel interpolation generalizes worse than early-stopped regression in large dimensions.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops theoretical bounds and numerical experiments for kernel regression under n ≍ d^γ; it does not reproduce the original deep-network model-size or epoch experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported rates and plateaus depend on the scaling exponent γ and the spherical inner-product-kernel/RKHS setting. Numerical experiments use NTK or fixed-bandwidth RBF kernels and select a stopping-time constant from a stated set.

fits_no_version.finding: For inner-product kernels on uniform spherical data with targets in the RKHS unit ball, the minimax excess-risk rate exponent varies non-monotonically in γ (n ≍ d^γ). Peaks fall at γ = 2, 4, 6, … and isolated valleys at γ = 3, 5, 7, …; early stopping attains these rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In high-dimensional kernel regression with n ≍ d^γ, the optimal excess-risk rate exponent shows multiple descent in γ.

fits_no_version.finding: Expressed in terms of d, the optimal rate stays constant over γ ∈ (1,2) ∪ (3,4) ∪ …, giving a 'periodic plateau'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High-dimensional kernel-regression rates show periodic plateaus as the sample-size/dimension exponent grows.

fits_no_version.finding: With NTK and RBF kernels, early-stopped kernel regression fits rates close to theory. Kernel interpolation is comparable at γ = 0.5 and slower at γ = 0.8, 1.5 and 1.8. For example, NTK at γ = 1.5 gives fitted slopes of 0.66 for regression versus 0.33 for interpolation (magnitudes).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In large-dimensional kernel regression, early-stopped estimators converge faster than kernel interpolation when γ > 1 / 0.8.

record.problems: The reported empirical study uses 20 repetitions and N = 1000 test points, but reports no error bars or intervals. The flattened figure-slope labels are ambiguous in sign, so numerical fitted slopes cannot be safely assigned. The theoretical and empirical results concern a specific high-dimensional kernel-regression setting and do not test the claim's stated axes.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the cited results of other papers. No rows for stopping-time constants tried only to choose a setting. Figure-only fitted slopes were omitted because their flattened labels have ambiguous signs; qualitative experimental statements are recorded in R5–R12.

untested.parts: No deep-network model-size sweep and no test error around the interpolation threshold.
No test error over training time. The stopping time is fixed at Θ(n^1/2) or chosen from a constant grid.
No sample-size sweep at fixed dimension near an interpolation threshold. n and d are linked by n = d^γ.
No risk-versus-capacity curve past the interpolation point for any model class.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak locations along size, epochs or samples.
The 'multiple descent' here is in the rate exponent over γ, not a risk peak along size, epochs or samples. It is not tied to label noise and is not shown removed by tuned regularization.
No re-counting of parameters or effective complexity that turns a second descent into a U-curve.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly linked to no version. The paper's 'multiple descent' shares a name with V6 but concerns a rate exponent along the n–d scaling exponent, not test-error peaks along the claim's axes. The flattened figure labels give fitted-slope magnitudes: NTK regression 1.09/0.84/0.66/0.56 versus interpolation 1.03/0.27/0.33/0.14; RBF regression 1.31/0.90/0.72/0.61 versus interpolation 1.23/0.27/0.32/0.14, for γ = 0.5, 0.8, 1.5, 1.8. The decay context implies these are negative slopes. They could be added to rows R5–R12 but bear on no version. The stopping constant C is chosen post hoc from a grid, and only the best result is shown.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size sweep and test error around the training-set interpolation threshold in deep networks.
Increasing sample size near a fixed interpolation threshold, with other relevant settings held fixed.
Risk versus model capacity across model classes, including behavior past an interpolation point.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations along size, epochs, or sample count.
Dependence of peaks on label noise or regularization, multiple peaks along the listed axes, and removal by optimally tuned regularization.
Whether re-counting complexity by effective parameters turns a second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: kernel regression with inner product kernels
rows.operation_detail: Derive minimax excess-risk rates under n ≍ d^γ for even integer γ.

conditions.value: unit ball of the associated RKHS

rows.value: Lower bound C1 n^−1/2 (Theorem 4.2(i)); early-stopped kernel-regression upper bound C1 n^−1/2 (Theorem 4.3(i)).
rows.uncertainty: The upper bound holds with probability at least 1 − C2 exp{−C3 n^1/2}; constants are not specified numerically.
rows.note: This is a rate result at specified γ values, not a model-size, epoch, or fixed-dimension sample-size sweep.

rows.subject: kernel regression with inner product kernels
rows.operation_detail: Derive minimax excess-risk rates under n ≍ d^γ.

conditions.value: unit ball of the associated RKHS

rows.value: Lower bound C1 n^−((γ−p)/γ + ϵ) for any ϵ > 0 (Theorem 4.2(ii)); early-stopped upper bound C1 n^−((γ−p)/γ) log(n) (Theorem 4.3(ii)).
rows.uncertainty: The upper bound holds with probability at least 1 − δ − C2 exp{−C3 n^(p/γ) log(n)}; the lower-bound constants depend on ϵ as stated.
rows.note: Rates are reported across a scaling-exponent interval, not along any listed claim axis.

rows.subject: kernel regression with inner product kernels
rows.operation_detail: Derive minimax excess-risk rates under n ≍ d^γ.

conditions.value: unit ball of the associated RKHS

rows.value: Lower bound C1 n^−((p+1)/γ) (Theorem 4.2(iii)); early-stopped upper bound C1 n^−((p+1)/γ) (Theorem 4.3(iii)).
rows.uncertainty: The upper bound holds with probability at least 1 − δ − C2 exp{−C3 n^(1−(p+1)/γ)}.
rows.note: The paper describes the rate curve as nonmonotone in γ, with peaks at γ = 2, 4, 6, ··· and isolated valleys at γ = 3, 5, 7, ···; those are scaling-exponent locations, not interpolation thresholds along model capacity.

source_check.locator_found: Theorems 4.2(iii), equation (16), and 4.3(iii), equation (19); discussion following Remark 4.5.

rows.subject: kernel regression with inner product kernels
rows.operation_detail: Describe how the optimal excess-risk rate varies with γ when expressed as a rate in dimension d.

conditions.value: unit ball of the associated RKHS

rows.measure: dimension-rate exponent of optimal excess risk
rows.value: The exponent ζ in the rate as a function of d stays invariant within the stated ranges; the text gives d = 10 and n from 10^7 to 10^8 as an example where the rate stays proportional to 10^−4.
rows.note: The plateau is as γ changes with n = d^γ, not a sample-size sweep at fixed dimension and interpolation threshold.

rows.subject: NTK kernel regression
rows.operation_detail: Estimate excess-risk convergence with n and d linked by n ≍ d^γ.
rows.value: Authors state that the kernel-regression convergence rate is consistently close to the theoretical rate; kernel interpolation is comparable at γ = 0.5.
rows.uncertainty: 20 repetitions are reported; no error bars or interval are stated.
rows.note: The figure's flattened fitted-slope labels are ambiguous in sign; no numerical slope is assigned. The scaling path varies dimension along with sample size.

relation.reason: The paper discusses related multiple-descent behavior and kernel interpolation, but its own rate-exponent results neither test a listed version nor use double descent as a tool.

tranche.reason: The results concern asymptotic convergence-rate exponents under n ≍ d^γ, rather than risk curves across model capacity, training epochs, or an interpolation threshold. They do not test any listed claim version.

source_check.notes: Peaks and valleys refer to the signed exponent in the power of n; the positive decay exponent has the opposite extrema. Pack values and uncertainty fields are truncated, so row checks cover visible content; Theorem 4.3(ii) includes a log(n) factor, and its lower bound matches only up to an arbitrary ε in the exponent.
